terms.definition: Software Development Life Cycle — a structured process with six phases (Requirement Analysis, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, Maintenance) that guides how software is built.
terms.example: Like a recipe for building software — you don't skip steps or change the order without consequence.

terms.definition: A sequential SDLC approach where each phase must be fully completed before the next begins. Rigid and difficult to change once started.
terms.example: Like building a house — you lay the foundation before walls, walls before roof. Going back is expensive.

terms.definition: An iterative, sprint-based SDLC approach where working software is delivered in short cycles with continuous feedback and adaptation.
terms.example: Like cooking a new recipe — taste and adjust as you go, rather than waiting until the full meal is done.

terms.definition: A set of instructions written in a programming language that a computer executes to perform a specific task.
terms.example: print('Hello World') is a one-line Python program that tells the CPU to display text.

terms.definition: One or more programs packaged together to solve a problem. Software runs on computers — it is not the end user.
terms.example: Microsoft Office = Word + Excel + PowerPoint + tools all packaged together.

terms.definition: Software specifically designed for an end user to perform a task through a user interface.
terms.example: WhatsApp, Gmail, and Amazon Shopping are applications — they're designed for you (the end user) to interact with.

terms.definition: Central Processing Unit — the brain of a computer that executes program instructions.
terms.example: Every time you open an app, the CPU is reading and executing millions of instructions per second.

terms.definition: Random Access Memory — temporary workspace that holds programs and data while they're actively running. Cleared when the computer shuts down.
terms.example: Think of RAM as your desk — you keep current work there, but clear it when you're done.

terms.definition: A device or software that requests resources or services from a server. Can be a machine (laptop, phone) or software (browser, app).
terms.example: Your browser (Chrome) is client software; your laptop is the client machine when you browse the web.

terms.definition: A powerful computer or software that provides resources, services, or data to clients in response to requests.
terms.example: AWS EC2 instances are server machines. Apache and Nginx are server software running on them.

terms.definition: A unique numerical identifier assigned to every device on a network, used to locate and route data to that specific device.
terms.example: Like a home address — 192.168.1.1 uniquely identifies a device so data packets know where to go.

terms.definition: A numbered endpoint on a server that identifies which specific service or application should receive incoming network traffic.
terms.example: Port 443 = HTTPS. Port 22 = SSH. Like apartment numbers — same building (IP), different residents (services).

terms.definition: A set of rules governing how data is formatted and transmitted between devices on a network.
terms.example: HTTP and HTTPS are protocols defining how browsers and web servers communicate.

terms.definition: Capital Expenditure — large, upfront one-time costs for purchasing physical assets like servers, storage, and networking equipment.
terms.example: Buying 10 servers for ₹50 lakhs is CapEx — you own them but pay a huge amount upfront.

terms.definition: Operational Expenditure — recurring costs incurred in day-to-day operations. Cloud converts CapEx to OpEx with pay-as-you-go pricing.
terms.example: Paying ₹5,000/month for cloud servers you actually use is OpEx — no upfront cost, scales with usage.

terms.definition: The delivery of IT resources — servers, storage, databases, networking, software — over the internet on a pay-as-you-go basis.
terms.example: Instead of buying a server, you rent one from AWS for $0.10/hour and stop paying when you turn it off.

terms.definition: Cloud Computing Service Provider — a company that delivers computing resources over the internet (e.g., AWS, Azure, GCP).
terms.example: AWS is the world's largest CCSP, offering 200+ cloud services used by Netflix, NASA, and millions of startups.

terms.definition: Amazon Web Services — the world's largest cloud computing platform, offering 200+ services across compute, storage, databases, networking, AI, and more.
terms.example: When you stream Netflix, the video is likely served from AWS data centers.

terms.definition: The ability to increase or decrease computing resources quickly and automatically based on demand.
terms.example: An app handling 100 users can scale to handle 100,000 users on cloud — in minutes, not weeks.

terms.definition: A cloud pricing model where you only pay for the resources you actually consume, with no upfront commitment or idle waste.
terms.example: Like a taxi — you pay for the ride you took, not for the taxi sitting in a garage waiting for you.

terms.definition: Software that handles HTTP/HTTPS requests from browsers and sends back web pages (HTML, CSS, JS).
terms.example: Apache and Nginx are popular web servers. They listen on port 80 (HTTP) and 443 (HTTPS).

terms.definition: Software that stores, organizes, and retrieves structured data in response to queries from application servers.
terms.example: MySQL and PostgreSQL store your app's data — user accounts, orders, products — in organized tables.

terms.definition: A practice combining software Development and IT Operations — focused on automating deployment, monitoring, and scaling of applications on cloud infrastructure.
terms.example: A DevOps engineer sets up the AWS infrastructure so developers can deploy their code and users can access it reliably.
